newsitem.title: YEMEN: Yemen counts votes amid charges of poll violations.
newsitem.headline: Yemen counts votes amid charges of poll violations.

text.p: Yemen continued counting votes into the early hours of Tuesday after the junior coalition partner in the government accused the ruling party of violating election rules by moving some ballot boxes to military camps.

The announcement of initial results in Yemen's first parliamentary elections since a 1994 civil war which nearly tore the country apart was expected by noon (0900) on Tuesday after a one-day delay caused by a high voter turnout, officials said.
Parliament speaker Sheikh Abdullah Bin Hussein Al-Ahmar of the Islah Party, an influential Islamist group, accused some ruling party members of hampering the count in many constituencies.

He insisted at a news conference in his hometown of Khamir, outside the capital Sanaa, that the announcement of first results was delayed because some General People's Congress (GPC) members, local officials and candidates wanted counting to be done in military camps instead of designated polling stations.
"The results are late because the GPC is hampering counting in many constituencies," he said.
"This is a violation of the law. It is evidence of bad intentions... We will not accept the transfer of ballot boxes."

Abdul-Aziz al-Saqqaf, secretary-general of the independent elections monitoring committee, said Al-Ahmar's charges were "within the scope of political manoeuvring that comes with the (election) baggage".
"It did happen...boxes from two centres were moved. If all the people monitoring those centres also moved it is not serious violations", he told Reuters late on Monday.
The GPC said in a statement late on Monday it had won in 33 constituencies and Islah claimed victory in eight others, but there was no independent confirmation of either claim.

Saeed al-Hekaimi, spokesman for the Supreme Election Committee, said turnout in the Sunday ballot had been high due to new voting cards which carried election symbols, enabling illiterate voters to take part.
Turnout was officially put at 80 percent although international monitors believed it was closer to 60 percent.
Voting was overshadowed by shootings in which nine died.
Witnesses said Sanaa appeared calm on Monday. Military police armed with rifles manned polling stations while votes were counted.

Hekaimi said voting would be repeated in a constituency in Dhamar, 100 km (60 miles) south of Sanaa after voters refused to cast ballots because the symbol of their candidate was missing due to an administrative error. He gave no new date.

Hekaimi also reported "a new incident of election violence in Dhamar" but declined to elaborate. An election observer told Reuters three people were wounded, two seriously, after supporters of the Dhamar candidate whose symbol was missing from ballot papers opened fire on a car carrying supporters of his rival.
Before voting began, a soldier opened fire on people at a polling area in the town of Mukayras, killing five soldiers and three civilians, Interior Minister Hussein Mohammad Arab said.
Also on Sunday, a man refused access to a polling station in Dhamar fired on a security officer who died after the attack.
Many Yemenis routinely carry guns. Violent incidents are often related to tribal strife.

The main opposition Yemen Socialist Party, some of whose former leaders launched the separatist campaign that sparked civil war, and three others boycotted the polls, alleging irregularities. The government denied the charges.
